front: How long should a patient be NPO before TEE?

back: Esophageal stricture, diverticulum, scleroderma, Mallory-Weiss tear, tumor, or trauma; known perforation of stomach or esophagus; active GI bleeding; recent GI/oropharyngeal surgery.

front: Are esophageal varices an absolute contraindication to TEE?
back: No — relative. Grade 1 varices are acceptable; grade 4 are not.

front: A patient becomes cyanotic after benzocaine spray during TEE — what is the diagnosis and treatment?
back: Methemoglobinemia (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺, low SaO₂ despite normal PaO₂). Treat with IV methylene blue 1% (10 mg/mL).

front: What are the two most common TEE complications?
back: Hoarseness and lip injury (each > 10%). Overall complication rate 0.18–2.8%; mortality < 0.02%.

front: Which TEE view angles best acquire mid-esophageal 4Ch, 2Ch, and LAX?
What is the TEE 'blind spot' of the aorta and why?
back: The distal ascending aorta and proximal arch — obscured by air in the trachea and main-stem bronchi that lie between the esophagus and this segment.

front: What LAA emptying velocity threshold is associated with thrombus and cardioembolic risk?
back: < 20 cm/s. Associated with severe spontaneous echo contrast and subsequent embolic events.

front: What is the sensitivity of TEE for aortic dissection?
Which imaging modality is the gold standard for confirming mitral annuloplasty ring dehiscence?
What position and probe orientation are used for TEE insertion?
back: Left lateral decubitus, moderate sedation, probe with anterior flexion. Inspect the probe and confirm a live image on screen before insertion.

front: If a TEE probe coils in the esophagus with the tip toward the mouth, what maneuver corrects it?
During transgastric TEE imaging, what maneuver is universally applied?
back: Always anteflex (both standard and deep transgastric views).

front: Where are LAA thrombi most commonly located?
back: At the tip of the appendage. They may be multilobulated. Pectinate muscles (visible around 100–110°) are the main mimic — should not be mistaken for thrombus.
The valve of the coronary sinus at its opening into the right atrium.
A muscular ridge between the LAA orifice and the left upper pulmonary vein. Normal anatomy — not a thrombus.

front: List four common causes of a dilated coronary sinus on echo.
back: 1) RA hypertension (severe TR, PH, RHF). 2) Coronary sinus fistula. 3) Anomalous pulmonary venous drainage to the CS. 4) Persistent left SVC draining to the CS.

front: Which pulmonary artery is NOT well visualized by TEE and why?
back: The left pulmonary artery — obscured by air in the left main-stem bronchus. Main PA and right PA are seen well.

front: During transseptal puncture, which TEE view provides the best A-P guidance?
back: Short-axis view at the level of the aortic root. The needle should be manipulated posterior to the aorta.
